problem: End-to-end RL image-goal navigation policies must learn planning, collision avoidance and stopping jointly, overfit to training scenes, and transfer poorly to real cluttered environments. Existing hierarchical methods (e.g. NTS) still learn navigation and collision avoidance together and are not validated on real robots.
motivation: Real-world image-goal navigation with only a goal image needs efficient exploration, robust obstacle avoidance and correct stopping. Decoupling these into separately designed or learned modules should improve generalization and ease sim-to-real transfer.
key_idea: Decompose image-goal navigation into four decoupled modules (mapping, RL-learned long-term goal prediction on the map, reactive motion planning, learned navigation-ending classifier) so the image-goal task becomes a sequence of point-goal tasks.
insight: Replacing the learned goal predictor with a random one drops overall SR from 0.57 to 0.51, so the learned long-term goal module matters. The dense exploration-based reward is essential: the sparse-reward variant (Ours-SR) fails to learn (0.23 SR). Merging motion planning and stopping into one local policy (Ours-LP) degrades on harder tasks (0.31 vs 0.43 SR on Hard). Swappable modules (Gmapping + CrowdMove on the real robot) enable direct sim-to-real transfer with far fewer collisions than end-to-end baselines.
method: Mapping module: Neural-SLAM in Habitat (using sensor poses, so maps are relatively noiseless) or laser Gmapping on the real robot, producing an 8-channel obstacle/explored/agent-position map.

Long-term goal prediction: siamese ResNet-18 (ImageNet-pretrained) embeds the panoramic observation and the goal image (fusion to 256-d); a 5-layer CNN encodes the map; a PPO actor-critic outputs a Gaussian over a 2-D long-term goal on the map every k=10 steps.

Reward: r = r_g (+20 if the predicted goal is within 1.0 m of the goal image) + r_collide (-5 if the goal is in an unreachable area) + an exploration-area-increment term that rewards exploring until the goal image enters the explored area, then penalizes further exploration.

Reactive motion planning: the Fast Marching Method (discrete actions) in Habitat; CrowdMove (a learned sensor-to-controls policy with continuous velocity) on the real robot; replanned at every step on the updated map.

Navigation ending prediction module: siamese ResNet-18 binary classifier on (current view, goal image) pairs, labeled 1 if their distance is <=1.0 m; trained with BCE jointly with the goal predictor on Habitat trajectories.
Training: 72 Gibson scenes for training, 14 for testing; parallel PPO with 72 episodes per update, 500 steps (50 time scales) per episode; about 24 h on 8 V100 GPUs.

setting.backbone: ResNet-18 siamese networks + CNN map encoder (PPO-trained long-term goal policy, BCE-trained ending classifier), Neural-SLAM/Gmapping, FMM/CrowdMove
setting.training_data: Habitat with Gibson, 72 training scenes, trained purely in simulation; ending-module pairs sampled from navigation trajectories
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (four 128x128 views at 0/90/180/270°) + sensor pose; laser scan on the real robot
setting.action_space: Habitat: discrete forward/turn left/turn right/stop; real robot: continuous velocity commands
setting.privileged: none (sensor pose used directly in simulation instead of pose estimation)

numbers.eval_set_note: 14 held-out Gibson scenes; 1000 tasks per difficulty level (Easy/Medium/Hard)
numbers.backbone: Neural-SLAM + ResNet-18 siamese goal predictor + FMM

numbers_note: Table 1 is on the 14 held-out Gibson scenes; the paper does not name the benchmark explicitly. Ablation variants (Ours-RP/SR/LP) omitted.
results: In Habitat, Ours_1 reaches overall SR 0.57 / SPL 0.35, beating TD-RL-ITR (0.44/0.22) and NTS on SR overall (0.55) and on Medium/Hard SR, though NTS is better on Easy (0.80/0.60) and overall SPL (0.38). On a real TurtleBot2, Ours_2 achieves higher SR and lower collision rate than all end-to-end baselines in all five configurations (e.g. 0.50/0.14 vs TD-RL-ITR 0.28/0.38).
limitations: The real-world SR is still modest (0.26–0.58), and performance drops on complex tasks because of the sim-to-real gap in the goal and ending modules.
Neural-SLAM does not transfer to the real robot, so a different mapping module (Gmapping with a laser) is needed, and sim uses sensor poses.
NTS could not be compared in the real world, and the motion planner suffers from freezing and collisions under sensor noise and actuation delay.
